items.title: A walker who halves their distance forever still reaches the wall
items.claim: Walk halfway to a wall. Then half of what's left. Then half again. Infinitely many steps — but the total distance is finite (the original distance), and the total time (if you halve your time at each step too) is also finite. Zeno's paradox resolved.

options.text: Infinity — there are infinitely many terms
Exactly 1. Geometric series with ratio r where |r| < 1 sums to a/(1-r); here a = 1/2 and r = 1/2, so sum = (1/2)/(1/2) = 1
Depends on how many terms you take

items.reveal:
A geometric series: a + ar + ar^2 + ar^3 + ... For |r| < 1, the sum is a/(1-r).

Proof: let S = a + ar + ar^2 + ... Then rS = ar + ar^2 + ar^3 + ... = S - a. So S - rS = a, giving S = a/(1-r).

Examples:
1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... = (1/2)/(1 - 1/2) = 1.
0.999... = 0.9 + 0.09 + 0.009 + ... = 0.9/(1 - 0.1) = 1.
1 + 1/3 + 1/9 + ... = 1/(1 - 1/3) = 3/2.

For |r| >= 1: the series diverges. 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + ... grows without bound.

Zeno's paradoxes resolved: Achilles catches the tortoise in finite time because the catching-up steps form a convergent series. Modern calculus formalises 'limit' and 'sum to infinity', tools Zeno did not have.

Applications:
- Compound interest formulas (sum of payment streams).
- Mortgage/loan calculations.
- Probability of getting heads eventually in repeated coin tosses.
- Resonance in physics (geometric series of wave reflections).
- Convergence of decimal expansions, power series, Taylor expansions.

Fermat, Newton, Leibniz, Cauchy, Weierstrass — the theory of convergent series was refined over centuries. By Weierstrass's epsilon-delta formalisation (1850s), 'infinite sum equals 1' had precise rigorous meaning.

Non-convergent series: harmonic 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + ... diverges (slowly, but to infinity). Conditional convergence (alternating series) raises subtle issues — Riemann showed you can rearrange a conditionally convergent series to sum to any value.
items.why: Infinite tasks seem impossible. They're not: infinite quantities can sum to finite values, given the right conditions. Calculus tamed Zeno's paradoxes and made motion mathematically describable.

items.title: Computers compute sine by adding up polynomials
items.claim: Your calculator can't 'compute sine'. It computes a polynomial that approximates sine very accurately. Specifically, sin(x) = x - x^3/6 + x^5/120 - x^7/5040 + ... The Taylor series gives any function as a sum of polynomial terms.

options.text: Polynomials and sine are always equal
Any analytic function f(x) can be expressed as a power series sum of f^(n)(a) * (x-a)^n / n!; truncating to a few terms gives a polynomial approximation with rigorously bounded error near x = a
Only sine has a Taylor series

items.reveal:
Taylor series: f(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + f''(a)(x-a)^2/2! + f'''(a)(x-a)^3/3! + ...

For analytic functions (most functions arising in physics and engineering), the series converges to f(x) within a radius of convergence around a.

Key examples around a = 0 (Maclaurin):
sin(x) = x - x^3/3! + x^5/5! - x^7/7! + ... (converges for all real x)
cos(x) = 1 - x^2/2! + x^4/4! - x^6/6! + ... (converges for all real x)
e^x = 1 + x + x^2/2! + x^3/3! + ... (converges for all real x)
ln(1+x) = x - x^2/2 + x^3/3 - ... (converges for |x| < 1)
1/(1-x) = 1 + x + x^2 + x^3 + ... (converges for |x| < 1, geometric)

For small x, truncating after a few terms gives good approximation. For sin(x), keeping x - x^3/6 gives error of about x^5/120; for x = 0.1, error ~ 10^(-8).

Calculators use TWO TRICKS:
1. Argument reduction: reduce sin(x) for large x to sin(x') where x' is in a small range, using periodicity and symmetries.
2. Polynomial approximation: minimax polynomials (Chebyshev-optimal) often beat Taylor for fixed precision.

Applications:
- Computer hardware (FPUs): implement transcendental functions via polynomial approximation.
- Numerical analysis: many algorithms (Newton-Raphson, Runge-Kutta) involve Taylor expansion.
- Physics: small-angle approximations (sin x ≈ x, cos x ≈ 1) are first-order Taylor.
- Perturbation theory in quantum mechanics: expansion of solutions around exactly-solvable cases.

Divergent Taylor series: some functions have Taylor series that converge only at a single point (formal series that don't represent the function). These appear in asymptotic analysis (Stirling's approximation, certain physics calculations).
items.why: Functions like sine seem 'analytical' or special. Computationally, they're polynomial approximations. The Taylor expansion is the practical universal interface between abstract functions and computers.

items.title: You cannot walk across all seven Königsberg bridges once
items.claim: Königsberg (now Kaliningrad) sat on two riverbanks and two islands connected by seven bridges. The town's puzzle: is there a route that crosses each bridge exactly once? Euler proved in 1735 that there isn't — and invented graph theory in the process.
items.prompt: What's the criterion for the puzzle to have a solution?

options.text: Bridges must be arranged in a circle
Every vertex (landmass) must have even degree (an even number of bridges), except possibly the start and end points; Königsberg has four landmasses, all of odd degree
Bridges must be the same length

items.reveal_title: Euler's 1735 paper — birth of graph theory
items.reveal:
Euler abstracted Königsberg to a 'graph': landmasses become vertices, bridges become edges. The puzzle asks for an 'Eulerian path' (a walk using every edge exactly once).

Euler proved: an Eulerian path exists if and only if at most 2 vertices have odd degree. (A circuit, starting and ending at the same vertex, requires every vertex to have even degree.)

Königsberg: north bank had 3 bridges, south bank 3, east island 5, west island 3. All four are odd. So no Eulerian path exists.

Euler's paper was the first to study a problem in what we now call topology — caring about connections, not distances. Graph theory grew into a major branch of mathematics: shortest paths, network flows, Internet routing, social networks, and more.

Two of Königsberg's bridges were destroyed in World War II; only three of the original seven remain. Today the puzzle has a valid Eulerian path.
items.why: Geometric puzzles often look like they need detailed measurement. Sometimes only the abstract topology matters — and Euler's degree condition makes the answer trivial once formalised.
